title: Thank you India, Jio aapne banaya
summary: India's largest IPO to date became a nationwide thank-you moment.
idea: Jio Platforms listed on the NSE on October 28, 2026 after an issue of ₹30,188 crore, per Jio's own thank-you post. Jio already had universal awareness, so the campaign treated the listing as a public thank-you rather than an introduction.
how: Jio ran an official thank-you creative, also printed in newspapers: “Thank you, India. Jio aapne banaya.” It says the public made India's largest IPO possible, shows three figures (1.40 crore applications, ₹30,188 crore issue size, 79.62 lakh shareholders) and a crowd of everyday Indians walking toward India Gate.
Outdoor in Mumbai and content across social media, creators and publishers carried the message.
Paparazzi pages including Viral Bhayani and Rupees changed their profile pictures and bios to Jio branding.
Listing-day celebrations included employee events and a drone show over Marine Drive.
A tribute message from Mumbai auto-rickshaw drivers also circulated in a news-style post dated October 28.
stat_label: listing gain over the ₹1,119 issue price (EVENTFAQS)
why: Gratitude suited a brand that hundreds of millions already use. The idea worked in print, outdoor and social at once, and fan and paparazzi pages extended it for free.
watchouts: Visibility is not the same as investor demand. Keep copy on the marketing moment and away from financial claims.
takeaway: When a brand is already known, a milestone is best told as thanks to the audience.

title: PhonePe 10th Anniversary Anthem
summary: Naming 70 crore users would take 980 days. The film made that the joke.
idea: PhonePe marked 10 years with an anthem film that thanks its 70 crore registered users. Shahu Supreme, who holds the Indian record of 494 words a minute, is challenged to name users at top speed. At that pace the roll call would take 980 consecutive days.
how: The film was conceptualised with Ogilvy.
The month-long campaign was led by PhonePe's Instagram handle and amplified on YouTube, X and LinkedIn.
For its fifth anniversary in 2021, PhonePe had posted a maths equation on Twitter and more than 30 brands joined the guessing and birthday wishes.
stat_label: to say 70 crore user names at 494 words a minute (Indian Television)
why: Data became the creative device. A number too large to picture turned into a stunt people could compute and share.
watchouts: Anniversary campaigns drift into corporate self-praise. This one avoided that by making the audience the subject.
takeaway: Turn a big number into something people can picture or calculate.
credits: Public credit on the film: Ogilvy.

images.caption: Frame from the anthem film, as shown in a news video. The megaphone announcing names is the film's core device. File 04.

title: AI so natural, you can't tell it's AI
summary: An 80-second Diwali film where a voice assistant is so natural that nobody can tell it is AI.
idea: Cartesia is a voice-AI company, and Nugget is the AI platform from Zomato's parent Eternal, sold to businesses for customer support and voice assistants (Inc42). The film shows the technology doing small jobs during Diwali week and ends on the line “AI so natural, you can't tell it's AI”, over the Cartesia x nugget by Zomato lockup.
how: The film cuts between Diwali-week moments, each carried by a calm voice and subtitles: a relative checking on preparations, a voice assistant asking the user to keep ₹45,000 in an account and setting a morning reminder, a woman's 7:30 PM salon appointment confirmed, and a Zomato delivery partner sorting out an address (Ashok Bhavan, house number 312).
An older relative then tells the voice it is beautiful, and it answers that it is just an AI.
A family gathering closes the film with the lockup. The lockup suggests Cartesia's voices power the Nugget agents.
why: Setting a technology partnership inside a festive family scene gives it a human face.
watchouts: Do not say Noise Culture made the film or the idea. Do not state results. Do not confuse it with Zomato's consumer Diwali film (the Have a WOW film with Saif Ali Khan), which is a separate campaign.
takeaway: Technology partnerships land better when the story is human first.
credits: Film and idea by the brands (Cartesia and Nugget by Zomato). Distribution went through multiple agencies.

title: Basseline (#VaselineHijacked)
summary: A legacy brand renamed itself after a creator's mispronunciation and let fans take over.
idea: A Korean skincare creator, Min Day Lee, pronounced the brand in a way that sounded like “Baseline”, and the clip spread as “Basseline”. Vaseline India adopted it.
how: Renamed its social presence to Basseline with no pitch.
Followed with #VaselineHijacked, invited remixes and named Hijack Icons.
Brought in retail partners Nykaa and Tira, and had the creator pick the first three winners.
why: The brand credited the creator and treated the moment as a conversation.
takeaway: Acknowledge, credit, invite remixes, recognise the best.

title: Melody Tiramisu (#Melodi)
summary: A ₹1 toffee turned a viral diplomatic moment into a limited-edition launch.
idea: After Prime Minister Modi gifted Melody to Italy's Prime Minister Meloni, the #Melodi meme returned and Melody sold out in many places on quick commerce.
how: Parle replied with “Sweetening relationships since 1983”.
Launched a limited-edition Melody Tiramisu on August 2 to 3, exclusive to Blinkit.
why: Wide coverage and a quick-commerce stock-out followed the limited edition launch.
watchouts: A political meme. It worked because Parle was an accidental beneficiary. Do not present political memes as a service.
takeaway: Turn attention into a scarce, purchasable product.

title: Infinix Note 50x (#QuestionTheNoise)

title: The Official Apology Statement Trend
summary: Brands posted mock apologies for being too good, then the format saturated.
idea: A faux corporate apology flips a serious format into humour and shows self-awareness.
how: Skoda, Volkswagen India, T-Series, Keventers, Haldiram's, Myntra and others posted their own versions.
why: Self-awareness and subversion of standard PR statements created rapid engagement.
watchouts: Briefs turned it into a calendar checkbox, critics warned it cheapens real apologies, and a Volkswagen dealership post drew backlash.
takeaway: Join a format in its first week or skip it.

title: The 12-Tonne KitKat Heist
summary: A stolen chocolate truck became a joke that brands, tourism boards and police forces joined for days.
idea: Nestlé confirmed that a truck carrying about 12 tonnes of KitKat, or 413,793 bars, was stolen in transit from a factory in central Italy to Poland. The brand answered with a line that thieves had taken the “have a break” message too literally, and the internet did the rest.
how: KitKat announced the theft on its own channels around March 28 to 29, with a straight face and a joke.

Brands posted mock “official statements”. Domino's UK offered condolences and hinted at a KitKat pizza on March 30. KFC called the chocolate a possible “12th herb and spice”. DoorDash blamed a “packaging error”, PayPal offered Purchase Protection and Lipton Ice Tea called it one way to take a break.

Indian accounts joined on March 31: Kerala Tourism said it had checked its backwaters, hill stations and beaches and none of the chocolate was there. Deccan Herald also lists IRCTC and UP Police among the participants.
On April 1, KitKat launched a Stolen KitKat Tracker where people could enter the 8-digit batch code on a bar to see if it came from the missing shipment.
stat_label: of KitKat stolen in transit, after which brands joined the joke (Nestlé via AFP)
why: A real, bizarre event with a ready-made brand pun. The “official statement” format was easy to copy and each joiner tied it to its own product. Many posts carried disclaimers so they would not be misread.
watchouts: It was a real theft. AFP quoted KitKat warning of possible shortages before Easter, while its official statement post says supply is not affected, so tone mattered. The statement format was the same one that saturated in the Official Apology trend, and a joke is only fresh for its first days. This belongs in the pitch as a speed and tone example, not as work by Noise Culture.
takeaway: React within 24 to 48 hours, tie the joke to your own product mechanic, and add a one-line disclaimer.
